rv.q: Whether you are a parent or not, the play leaves you an abundance of ideas on which to ruminate.
This is a brilliant, chilling and genuinely provocative new play.

It is a plaintive piece, heavy with fond memories and unspoken regrets – remote as Butterwoth, cruel as Pinter, but sad too; a deep-tissue sadness that can’t be staved off with superficial pleasures and parsnip wine.

Robin and Hazel are two retired nuclear scientists living on the edge of an exclusion zone set up in light of a cataclysmic event that occurred at the nuclear plant where they used to work — leaving the surrounding area with dangerous levels of radiation.
For now, Kirkwood’s masterly play resonates with macrocosmic power, towering over the minutiae of living.

cn.t: Kirkwood's intimate three-hander impresses with its ability to raise big questions about generational responsibility and nuclear legacy through domestic drama. Strong performances and naturalistic staging elevate this smaller-scale but thought-provoking follow-up to Chimerica.
